events.title: The martyrdom of St. Cyprian of Carthage
events.shortBlurb: The bishop and great writer of the African Church was beheaded before his people in the persecution of Valerian…
body: Thascius Caecilius Cyprianus, born about 210 of a wealthy pagan family of Carthage and won to Christ in middle life, was chosen bishop of that city about 249. He guided the African Church through the Decian persecution, the bitter controversy over the readmission of the lapsed, and a wasting plague, and disputed with Pope Stephen I over baptism conferred by heretics.

When the Emperor Valerian renewed the persecution, Cyprian was examined on 30 August 257 by the proconsul Aspasius Paternus and banished to Curubis. Recalled the next year under a sterner edict, he waited quietly in his gardens until the guard came; on 14 September 258 the proconsul Galerius Maximus read the sentence, that Thascius Cyprian should die by the sword. Cyprian answered, 'Deo gratias' — Thanks be to God.

Before a vast crowd of his people he knelt and was beheaded outside the city, having bidden his friends give the executioner twenty-five gold pieces. His deacon Pontius wrote his Life, and the court record of his trial, the Acta proconsularia, survives entire. The first African bishop to win the martyr's crown, he is kept on 16 September together with Pope Cornelius, his ally and fellow martyr.

events.title: The dedication of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre
events.shortBlurb: Constantine's great basilica over Calvary and the tomb of Christ was dedicated at Jerusalem, giving rise to the feast of the Holy Cross…
body: After his victory over Licinius Constantine wrote to Macarius, bishop of Jerusalem, ordering a basilica surpassing all others over the tomb of Christ; the temple of Venus that Hadrian had planted over the site was torn down, and the tomb laid bare. Over the holy places rose the great Martyrium basilica, the courtyard about Calvary, and the rotunda of the Anastasis, which Eusebius called a New Jerusalem.

In 335, at the close of the Council of Tyre, Constantine bade the assembled bishops pass on to Jerusalem for the consecration, which fell on 13 and 14 September, and Eusebius himself pronounced the orations. On the second day, tradition records, Bishop Macarius lifted up the wood of the Cross before the people; and the anniversary, the Encaenia, was kept for eight days, drawing monks from Mesopotamia, Syria, and Egypt.

The church stood until the Persian sack of 614, and, rebuilt by the monk Modestus, until the caliph al-Hakim razed it in 1009. The church of the Crusaders, consecrated in 1149 over Calvary and the tomb, is the one that pilgrims enter today, nearly seventeen centuries after the bishops of Tyre kept the first Encaenia.

events.title: The death of St. John Chrysostom in exile
events.shortBlurb: The great preacher and archbishop of Constantinople died on the road of a second banishment, blessing God to the end…
body: John, born at Antioch about 349 and ordained its priest in 386, preached there for twelve years with such power that men called him Chrysostom, the 'golden-mouthed.' Made archbishop of Constantinople in 398, he reformed a worldly clergy and rebuked the court without fear, earning the enmity of the Empress Eudoxia and of Theophilus of Alexandria, who had him deposed at the Synod of the Oak in 403.

Briefly recalled, he was banished again in 404 to Cucusus in Armenia, whence his letters still heartened the Church. In the summer of 407 he was ordered to Pityus, at the far end of the Black Sea; marched on foot through heat and storm, he sank at Comana in Pontus and died there on 14 September 407. His last recorded words were 'Glory to God for all things.'

In 438 the Emperor Theodosius II, son of the Eudoxia who had exiled him, brought his relics to Constantinople and laid them in the Church of the Holy Apostles, begging pardon for his mother. East and West venerate him as a Doctor of the Church; and because 14 September belongs to the Holy Cross, the West keeps his feast on the thirteenth.
